content.text:
Fighting Style feats in DnD 5.5 are available as a class feature for many
	martial classes or as a feat, giving you ways to boost your preferred combat
	tactics. Many of these are reliable passive benefits which will benefit for
	you for your whole career. Some Fighting Styles will lock you into using
	specific equipment, but most characters don’t change equipment often enough
	for that to be an issue.
This article is for the 2024 DnD 5.5 rules. For the 2014 rules, see our
2014 DnD 5e Fighting Styles Guide

sections.heading: Getting a Fighting Style in DnD 5.5

content.text:
Fighting Style feats are available as a class feature for several classes and
	subclasses, or as a feat. However, since Fighting Style feats don’t come with
	an Ability Score Increase, it’s often hard to justify in one of your limited
	feat slots.

Champion Fighters gain a second Fighting Style at level 7, making them the
	only class or subclass that gets a second Fighting Style without multiclassing
	or feats.

The obvious choice for ranged builds. +2 to hit is a big deal in a game where
	a 20th-level character can expect a maximum of +11 to hit. The math of the
	game gives you a roughly 65% chance to hit when attacking a CR-appropriate
	creature with average AC, and raising that to 75% feels very satisfying. If
	you want to take the Sharpshooter feat, this is an absolute must.

If you’re considering a thrown weapon build, see Thrown Weapon Fighting,
	below, for a discussion on which fighting styles make sense for thrown
	weapons. Note that Archery applies to “attacks with ranged weapons,” not
	“ranged weapon attacks,” so there’s some frustrating nuance there.
Complementary Feats: Crossbow Expert, Gunner, Sharpshooter.
Complementary Weapons: Bows, Crowssbows, Darts, Firearms.

This one is hard. Blindsight, even at just 10-foot range, is extremely
	useful. It solves issues of invisible enemies, it helps make up for lack of
	magical options for Darkvision, and it addresses effects which block line of
	sight like fog, magical darkness, or other stuff. But those effects don’t
	appear in most encounters, so this is only situationally useful. When it works
	it’s great, but the rest of the time it’s useless. Unless you have allies in
	the party who plan to frequently use magical darkness or other options to
	obscure vision, I would skip this.

Races which suffer from Sunlight Sensitivity might consider this as a
	solution to their sunlight issues. If you don a blindfold (or close your
	eyes), your DM may allow you to overcome the effects of Sunlight Sensitivity
	by willingly blinding yourself. The text of Sunlight Sensitivity isn’t
	perfectly clear if it only applies to attacks which rely on sight, so this may
	not work RAW, but the idea makes sense.
Complementary Feats: None.
Complementary Weapons: Anything with reach.

Not very exciting, but since AC scales so little in 5e, a +1 can be a big
	difference. Defense also doesn’t lock you into using one type of weapon, so if
	you like to change weapons to suit the situation, Defense can be a great
	choice. It’s also helpful if you don’t plane to use weapons in any meaningful
	way, making it a great choice for spellcasers multiclassing into martial
	classes.

2 damage closes the damage gap between a longsword and a two-handed weapon
	like a greataxe or greatsword (4.5 improves to 6.5 vs. 6.5/7), so you can have
	the damage of a two-handed weapon with the AC of sword-and-board. It’s not
	fancy and it doesn’t change your tactics, but it always works and the damage
	bonus is reliable.
Note that this works while using a shield, and it’s intended to do so.

It’s unclear how this interacts with thrown weapons. The bonus applies “when
	you’re holding a Melee weapon in one hand and no other weapons.” If you throw
	the weapon, do you still get the damage bonus? The weapon is no longer in your
	hand when you hit, which is the closest I can find to an actual answer. I
	don’t think Dueling is intended to work with thrown weapons, especially now
	that we have the Thrown Weapon Fighting style.
Complementary Feats: Defensive Duelist, Shield Master.
Complementary Weapons: Longsword, Rapier, similar one-handed weapons.

This adds an average of just over 1 damage per attack on average with a
	greatsword, and even less for other weapons. If you plan to use two-handed
	weapons, I generally recommend that you pick up Defense instead to compensate
	for lack of a shield.

It appears that you can roll any damage die that’s part of the attack.
	Secondary sources of damage, such as Divine Smite and other smite spells, may
	not qualify.
Complementary Feats:
Great Weapon Master
Polearm Master
Complementary Weapons: Greatsword, Maul, Double-Bladed Scimitar.

Conceptually similar to Protection, but there’s some nuance in how the two
	styles protect your target. Protection imposes Disadvantage, so if there’s a
	good chance that the attack would miss, it’s the better choice. Interception
	reduces the damage and always works, but for big attacks it won’t negate the
	whole attack.

The decision between the two comes down to who you’re going to be protecting.
	If you’re protecting other allies with decent AC (a melee cleric or rogue, for
	example), go for Protection. If you’re protecting allies with awful AC (most
	wizards), Disadvantage won’t help much, so go for Interception.
Complementary Feats: None.
Complementary Weapons: Anything with reach or range.

It’s nice that the damage bonus applies regardless of weapon, but relying on
	allies’ positioning means that it will only be reliable if you drag an ally
	around. Mounted combat is your best choice, but that will never get you the +2
	bonus. If you try to get another ally to take this so that you can get the +2
	bonus, you will both spend every combat chasing each other around trying to
	qualify for the damage bonus, and you’ll frequently lose it as enemies are
	killed or any time someone moves. A more consistent damage bonus like Dueling
	will be much more reliable.
Complementary Feats: Mounted Combatant.
Complementary Weapons: None.

This makes being Prone purely beneficial: you don’t suffer any penalties, and
	it’s no longer easier for enemies to hit you in melee. Enemies still have
	Disadvantage to attack you at range, so being Prone become actively
	beneficial. You still need to spend half of your movement to stand, which can
	be a huge pain, but Athlete reduces that cost from hald your speed to just 5
	feet, essentially removing it.

This could be useful for ranged builds fighting from far enough away that you
	don’t need to worry about enemies getting into melee with you, but it likely
	won’t be impactful in many fights because relatively few enemies rely on
	ranged attacks.
Complementary Feats: Athlete.
Complementary Weapons: None.

Tempting for Defender builds, but allies need to remain adjacent to you for
	this to work. Being adjacent to the front line tank is generally a bad place
	to be unless you can do so safely without someone defending you.

This also appeals to mounted combat builds because you can use it to
	compensate for your mount’s relative fragility, but if you’re going that
	route, you really need the Mounted Combatant feat which lets you retarget
	attacks to yourself instead.
Complementary Feats: Shield Master.
Complementary Weapons: Whip (for reach while using a shield).

Superior Technique hasn’t been updated to the 5.5 rules. The updated version
	of Fighting Style gives you access to the Fighting Style category of feats,
	but Superior Technique isn’t a feat. Your DM might still allow you to take it,
	but it’s not great.

A small damage boost to thrown weapons. The damage boost brings thrown
	weapons closer to ranged weapons like bows and crossbows. But that raises an
	important question: why take a Fighting Style just to be as good as a weapon
	without a Fighting Style? 5e didn’t really have an answer, but 5.5’s Weapon
	Masteries add a lot of utility to thrown weapons. The ability to change
	masteries with every attack offers a ton of potential utility. You can also
	use them one-handed, leaving your other hand free for a shield.

The biggest problem with thrown weapons is the ammunition. Throw weapons are
	considerably heavier than arrows, and your DM might start to question how
	you’re carrying dozens of daggers, javelins, axes, and whatever else. You
	either need to carry a ton of them, or you need Returning weapons.

Thrown Weapon Fighting has some unique interactions with other fighting
	styles. If you use a melee weapon with the Light and Thrown property like
	handaxes, you can benefit from the Two-Weapon Fighting style and from the Nick
	Weapon Mastery. If you take the Dual Wielder feat, you can upgrade to Javelins
	for extra range and you can get an extra attack as a Bonus Action.

If you instead use ranged weapons with the Thrown property, you can benefit
	from the Archery style, adding +2 to attacks. This allows you to match the
	average damage of a longbow while still holding a shield and fighting at
	range, so it makes sense to think of the Fighting Style as a +2 AC bonus and
	comparing that to the +2 attack bonus from Archery. Unfortunately, the only
	qualifying weapon is Darts, and limiting yourself to one weapon removes the
	most appealing part of thrown weapons.
Complementary Feats:
Dual Wielder
, Sharpshooter.

Complementary Weapons: Daggers, Darts, Hand Axes, Light Hammers, Javelins,
	Spears, Tridents.

Fighting with two weapons gets you an extra attack, but it’s not especially
	impactful without your ability modifier or some other damage boost like
	Hunter’s Mark. This makes fighting with two weapons much more impactful, but
	it’s absolutely not worth taking if you don’t also use a Nick weapon.
Complementary Feats:
Dual Wielder

Complementary Weapons: Anything with the Light property. Just try to match
	the damage types so that you can also take a matching feat.

Unless you’re benefiting from the bonus grapple damage, this is worse than
	just using a warhammer, so if you take this style, expect to lean heavily into
	the
Grapple+Shove
combo.
Complementary Feats: Grappler, Skill Expert.
Complementary Weapons: None.
